What Did You Really See on Ayahuasca? - Wednesday: Maamar Yafeh Sha'ah Achas #9
blurb: What Does It Feel Like to Burn in Hell? Can I Trust the G-d Who Created It? Can I Trust the G-d Who Created Hell? Are There Really Fires in Hell? How can we heal our trauma around paradise and purgatory? For many of us, the words Gan Eden and Gehenna evoke a terrifying picture of God and the afterlife. Even when we question that picture intellectually, our bodies may still brace for punishment every time we make a mistake. This class returns to the very language that frightened us, including the Talmud’s teaching that earthly fire is one-sixtieth of the fire of Gehenom. Through the Mitteler Rebbe’s maamar, we explore purgatory as the experience of having our own lives reflected back to us with a clarity we can't always perceive in this world. There is the pain of losing a mask we mistook for our skin. And there is the deeper grief of discovering how much of our passion went into securing a feeling of love or validation at the cost of our own truth. Why can an affair feel so alive to a person who has felt invisible for years? What happens when that same person can finally feel both the warmth they craved and what they sacrificed to get it? When we discover how we betrayed our own souls, we feel compelled to purge. The pain is profound, and it is followed by paradise and redemption. title: Mitteler Rebbe's Padah Beshalom part 6/9 שערי תשובה ד"ה פדה בשלום (פרק ז-ח)
blurb: Link to מאמר PDF⁠⁠ Finishing the explanation of חיה, the מיטעלער רבי demonstrates how the strong ביטול of the נפש הבהמית to the נפש האלקית is merely a ביטול of its רצון, and not of the actual נפש, which means that the נפש might still revert back to its original status. The מיטעלער רבי then introduces the level of יחידה by first explaining the level of "השתוות" equilibrium. To explain this, the מיטעלער רבי launches into a fascinating exploration of the two polar experiences at a person's core being - pleasure and pain. The מיטעלער רבי explains how pain is only experienced by lack of pleasure, and as much pleasure as a person has from any given experience will dictate how much pain they will feel from the absence of that pleasure.
